title: Infra Playbook: GPU fleet capacity, networking, Terraform & CI/CD (addendum 2026)
author: Sofia Ramirez
summary: Addendum to the canonical GPU fleet playbook: distilled operational procedures for capacity, cloud account networking, IaC module patterns, CI/CD gating, and runbooks for incidents.
body:
Overview
This addendum synthesizes lessons learned from recent scale events and CI/CD improvements. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform teams responsible for capacity planning, module design, and incident response.

Scope
- GPU fleet capacity planning and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account and networking patterns for inference clusters and control plane
- Terraform/IaC module authoring standards and examples
- CI/CD pipelines for infra code, AMI/container build, and release gating
- Runbooks and step-by-step procedures for common operational tasks

Owners and SLAs
- Primary owner: Infra Engineering (team: gpu-fleet)
- Secondary owner: Eng SRE (team: serving-sre)
- Business SLI targets: 99.95% cluster availability for dedicated capacity and 99.9% for shared pools (monthly).
- Operational SLOs: 95th percentile request scheduling latency < 500ms, pod start time for GPU nodes < 120s for scale-up events.

Key Metrics to Monitor
- GPU utilization per-instance (GPUs/instance): target steady-state 55-75%
- Cluster-level spare capacity: 10-20% buffer for burst/eviction events
- Pod scheduling failures per hour: target < 1
- Scale-up frequency: track number of autoscale events; frequent spikes indicate insufficient baseline capacity
- Cost per vGPU-hour vs observed throughput (tokens/sec or inferences/sec)

Capacity Model (Clarifications)
1. Baseline pool sizing: size pools to absorb 85% of the 95th-percentile sustained load without scale-up.
2. Burst capacity: maintain a pre-warmed burst pool sized to 10-15% of peak; automate warm-up based on forecasted traffic windows.
3. Autoscaler policy: cooldown 300s, max scale-up per-minute cap, and staggered node launches to prevent stampedes.
4. Preemption: designate explicit preemptible pools with automated routing fallbacks and graceful eviction handlers.

GPU Types and Node Sizing
- Recommended families: A100-80GB for high-throughput, A10/A30 for mid-tier, H100 for latency-sensitive and very large-model inference.
- Prefer single-GPU nodes where practical (1 GPU per node) for fastest drain and best bin-packing unless performance testing supports multi-GPU.
- Fractional-GPU strategies (MIG/runtime multiplexing) for stable low-memory models only.

Autoscaling and Pool Topologies
- Pool categories: reserved-dedicated, burst, spot-preemptible, and control/CPU-only.
- Routing: prefer reserved-dedicated -> burst -> preemptible. Canary traffic lands on reserved-dedicated or dedicated canary pools.
- Draining policy: graceful drain with --grace-period >= 300s to allow KV cache checkpointing and state flush.

Cloud Accounts and Networking Patterns
- Account segmentation: control-plane, shared infra, customer-dedicated. Enforce org-wide IAM guardrails and SCPs.
- VPC layout: per-region shared VPC with segmented subnets (control, serving, monitoring, management).
- Subnet sizing: default /20 for serving pools; increase where heavy IP churn is expected.
- Network security: restrict GPU nodes to egress-only to S3/object stores and control-plane endpoints; ops bastions handle admin access.
- Private endpoints: enable VPC interface endpoints for telemetry and data stores in Private deployments.

Terraform / IaC Conventions (refinements)
- Module layout: terraform-modules/<domain>/<module-name>/ (e.g., terraform-modules/gpu/eks-node-pool).
- Versioning: semver; breaking changes require major bump and migration notes.
- Inputs/outputs: favor explicit inputs, provide sensible defaults, and document outputs clearly in README.
- State: per-environment encrypted backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock). CI service account for applies; no personal credentials.
- Policy as code: enforce with OPA/Rego or tf-guard in pipeline.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines (improvements)
- Pipeline types: module lint/test/publish, artifact build (AMI/container), infra apply, canary promotion.
- Gates: tflint, tfsec, unit tests, integration apply in dev, and manual approval for prod.
- Immutable artifacts: publish AMIs/containers with digest tags and store metadata in artifact registry.
- Steps for terraform modules:
  1) checkout + pre-commit hooks
  2) terraform fmt & validate
  3) tflint and tfsec scans
  4) terraform plan against ephemeral/dev remote state
  5) apply in dev (auto-approve for non-prod), followed by PR and release tag for prod promotion

Release & Rollout
- Canary: target 5-10% fleet or a dedicated canary pool for 1-2 hours; monitor scheduling latency, pod restarts, and key accuracy metrics.
- Rollback automatic: trigger on critical alarms (pod crashloop > 5% or scheduling failures > 1/minute).

Runbooks: Procedures (condensed)
1) Scale-up failure (nodes stuck provisioning)
   - Pager: cluster-provision-fail
   - Steps:
     1. Check autoscaler logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler
     2. kubectl get nodes | grep NotReady; kubectl describe node <node>
     3. Inspect cloud console for launch errors (quotas, limits, subnet).
     4. Remediate quotas or subnet exhaustion; temporarily enlarge baseline pool if needed.
     5. Replace failed nodes and drain: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=300

2) GPU OOMs / Model crashes
   - Pager: gpu-oom-alerts
   - Steps:
     1. kubectl logs -p <pod> -c serving and capture inputs and KV cache size.
     2. Reduce batch size and restart with stricter resource limits.
     3. Route traffic away from affected pool; enable fallback model routing.
     4. Open incident with logs and remediation plan.

3) Draining pool for maintenance
   - Pre-checks: verify spare capacity and run canary smoke tests.
   - Steps:
     1. Set pool weight to 0 in routing (redwoodctl routing set --pool <pool> --weight 0).
     2. Evict pods gracefully and wait for KV checkpoints.
     3. Replace nodes and validate metrics.
     4. Re-enable pool and run acceptance tests.

Emergency Scale-Out Playbook (30-minute objective)
- Trigger: sustained queue depth > 2x expected > 3 minutes and spare capacity < 5%
- Owner: oncall SRE
- Steps:
  1) Manually increase desired_count for reserved pools via infra pipeline (use rollback-safe commit).
  2) Provision short-lived burst pool in alternate account/region if quotas block scale.
  3) Route non-critical customers to preemptible pool and throttle heavy users.
  4) Post-incident: capacity postmortem and baseline adjustment.

Testing, Validation, and Chaos
- Unit tests: terraform validate, tflint, tfsec, terratest unit mocks.
- Integration: apply in ephemeral dev account and run smoke harness (inference, KV persistence).
- Chaos: run node-termination and network-partition experiments in staging regularly.

Maintenance and Upgrade (Node image / driver)
1. Build new AMI/container with updated drivers.
2. Deploy to canary node pool (1-2 nodes) and run e2e checks for 2 hours.
3. Roll through pools in 10% increments with health checks.
4. Roll back immediately on regression.

Docs and Wiki Practice
- Ensure terraform module READMEs are comprehensive and include example usage.
- Maintain per-region capacity spreadsheet in team wiki, refreshed weekly.

FAQ (short)
- Q: When to use preemptible?
  A: For cost-sensitive, non-latency-critical workloads; critical models should be on reserved-dedicated pools.
- Q: How to remediate IP exhaustion?
  A: Move pools to /20 subnets, scale NAT gateways, and consider IPv6 for control-plane endpoints.

Appendix: Useful Commands
- kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=300
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Events:/,$p'
